---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB, and, as a hint only, when planning an audit's scope and worksets."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

Raw bindings that are a module of the crate, not a crate of their own, laid out and
generated as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, are named to `--sys-crates`
by their path, `crate::<path>`, beside the `-sys` crates that remain. A named module joins
the inventory and leaves every other counter, as a `-sys` crate does. Left unnamed, its C
types and functions are in no inventory, the cells that read it are taken over the other
crates' alone, and the generated code counts as the crate's own, all with no error. A module
that holds hand-written code beside its declarations is left unnamed, since naming it would
take that code out of the scan.

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as
ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters
that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts,
or subtracted from it. `--sites <counter> ...` also lists where each named counter's
increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named
before it. The counters that recur:

- `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which
  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in
  their signatures;
- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together
  `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their
  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;
- `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their
  `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions
  ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`,
  `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same
  of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows,
  slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change
  while they live;
- `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`,
  each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread;
- `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer
  the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live
  reference; and
- `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and
  tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those
  that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two
  leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`.

ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it
covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference
or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or
`from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source.

What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there.

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

---
name: ffibox
description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one."
---

# ffibox

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.

Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.

## Binding and porting

Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`,
`docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too.

### Binding types

A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they
apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them.

### Binding types › Safe layout

While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`,
and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle
routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`, and `CArc<Foo, P>` for `FooArc`. A
value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal<Foo, P>`.

### Binding symbols › Functions

A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned
through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's
iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a
borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half
is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C
half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only
inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier,
`callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body.
A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a
`CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as
`docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of
hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table.

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the
policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held
by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is
a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C.

### Porting › FFI boundary

An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does
with the Rust it reaches:

- the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`,
  `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return
  its owners and handles;
- memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C
  frees it through an exported release;
- a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a
  `CPayload`; and
- the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`.

## Testing

### Testing › UB tests

The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the
crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of
it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test.

## Reviewing

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.

Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.

## Binding and porting

Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`,
`docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too.

### Binding types

A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they
apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them.

### Binding types › Safe layout

While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`,
and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle
routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`, and `CArc<Foo, P>` for `FooArc`. A
value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal<Foo, P>`.

### Binding symbols › Functions

A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned
through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's
iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a
borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half
is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C
half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only
inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier,
`callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body.
A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a
`CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as
`docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of
hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table.

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the
policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held
by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is
a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C.

### Porting › FFI boundary

An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does
with the Rust it reaches:

- the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`,
  `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return
  its owners and handles;
- memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C
  frees it through an exported release;
- a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a
  `CPayload`; and
- the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`.

## Testing

### Testing › UB tests

The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the
crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of
it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test.

# Outbound Outbound is Rust's side of the boundary: memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. The inbound documents, [ownership.md](ownership.md) and [borrows.md](borrows.md), cover memory C owns held from Rust; this one walks the other way, with the same terms. ffibox is needed only where C **aliases** a value: keeps a pointer to it after a call returns, frees it, or calls back into it. A pointer passed down for one call and not kept is plain Rust: `&mut x as *mut _` for C that writes, `&x as *const _` for C that only reads, a `&CStr` or a slice's `as_ptr()`. ## The primitives | C does | Primitive | Rust counterpart | |--------|-----------|------------------| | frees an object or buffer Rust allocated | an owner under `RustAlloc`, surrendered with `into_raw` / `into_c` | `Box::into_raw` | | frees a string or buffer with its own allocator | `CStrBox::from_c_str`, `CVec::from_slice`, `CVec::from_fn`, `CVec::new_uninit` under that allocator's policy | `CString`, `Vec` | | frees a value or buffer Rust built, and grew, in C's allocator | `Box>` / `Vec>`, into a `CBox` / `CVec` and surrendered with `into_c` / `into_raw_parts` | `Box::new_in`, `Vec::new_in` | | calls a closure during one call | `CClosure`: `ctx()` and `trampoline()` | `&mut F` | | keeps a closure or value, and releases it later | `CPayload`: `into_raw()`, `release_fn()`, `trampoline()` | `Box` | | hands Rust a function and its context to call | `CFn` for the call or borrow it came with, `CFnBox` with the routine that releases the context: `call()`, `parts()` / `into_raw()` | a closure | | holds a callback that is either a Rust closure or a C function | `CCallback` (for a call or borrow), `CCallbackBox` (kept until released): `call()` from Rust, `c_form()` / `into_c()` to C | `impl FnMut`, `Box` | | calls into a table of function pointers, each slot passed the table (a backend, a stream) | `CTable`, its slots from `impl_cvtable!`: `as_c_ptr()` / `into_c()`, released through its `release` slot | `Box` | | returns an object through an out-parameter | `CBox::from_c_out`, `CStrBox::from_raw_out` | a return value | | calls a Rust routine that must not unwind into it | `callback::barrier` | `catch_unwind` | | frees, copies or constructs a ported type's objects | `export_cdrop!`, `export_cdupclone!`, `export_cnew!` | the C routines they replace | ## Choosing a primitive - **C frees it.** The memory comes from the allocator C frees with. If that is C's own (`free`, `lib_free`), build it through that allocator's policy: `CVec::from_fn` and `CVec::new_uninit` with a `CLenAlloc` policy, `CVec::from_slice` and `CStrBox::from_c_str` with a copying one, or a `Box` / `Vec` over `CAllocator

` when Rust builds or grows it natively, converted into a `CBox` / `CVec` to hand over. If C frees it through a Rust routine, allocate with `RustAlloc` and offer the release with `export_cdrop!`. Then surrender it with `into_raw`. - **C calls back during the call** (`foreach`, `qsort_r`). `CClosure::new` over `&mut F`. The trampoline's type is inferred from the C declaration it is passed to, and the closure's arguments are the C types, which the binding converts to handles before calling its consumer's closure. With `std`, a panic stops the C routine through the failure value and resumes after it, at `finish()`; a re-entrant invocation is refused the same way. `F: Send` unless the routine calls back on the calling thread only (`unsafe CClosure::new_local`). - **C keeps the callback** (`set_log_callback(cb, ctx, free)`). `CPayload` over an `Fn` closure, surrendered with `into_raw`, released by C through `release_fn()`. C may call it from several threads or re-entrantly, so it is reached as `&F`, and `into_raw` requires `Send + Sync`; state it changes goes behind a `Mutex` or an atomic. A panic in it aborts, so a fallible body goes in `barrier`. - **C keeps a value** (a container's payload, user data). `CPayload`, and `CPayload::borrow` inside the callbacks that receive it. - **C hands Rust a callback** (an options struct's `progress_cb` and `payload`, a ported function's `cb, ctx` arguments through its export). `CFn::new`, `unsafe`, states what the C that supplies the pair guarantees; `call((args…))` takes C's argument types, the context left out, so the binding's safe callable converts its arguments and calls in one justified block. `parts()` hands the pair to another C routine unchanged, with no trampoline between. - **A callable is either** (a field a consumer sets with a closure and C sets with a function, a callback ported code calls whoever supplied it). `CCallback` / `CCallbackBox` hold whichever it is: called from Rust, a closure runs through its trampoline, with the same refusal and panic handling as when C calls it, and handed to C, a C function goes as its own pair. - **C calls into a table Rust implements** (`git_config_backend`, a `git_writestream`: a struct of function pointers, each passed the table). `CTable`, the state `S` behind the table of the layout type `T`, whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints from the trait `S` implements: each slot declares its receiver, `&S` or `&mut S`, which decides what re-entry it allows, and its results for a panic and a refusal. C releases it through the slot declared `release`. [vtables.md](vtables.md) walks through it. A family of hooks C calls with no pointer back (`git_allocator`) is not a table: trampolines generic over the implementing type, in `barrier`. - **C returns something through an out-parameter.** `from_c_out` / `from_raw_out`: the slot starts NULL and is adopted whatever the routine returns, so an object handed over on failure is still released. - **C still frees a type Rust now allocates** (a port in progress). `export_cnew!` / `export_cdrop!` / `export_cdupclone!` with the type's policy, in the module's `ffi_export` gateway, so that C allocates and frees through Rust's allocator, never `malloc` / `free` crossed with it. ## Conventions - **Surrendering is safe, adopting is `unsafe`**, inbound and outbound alike: `into_raw` gives a pointer away, `from_raw` asserts what it addresses. - **What one allocator allocates, only it frees.** The policy in the owner's type enforces it on the Rust side; an export, by naming the policy, on C's. - **No unwinding into C.** A panic that reaches an `extern "C"` function aborts; `barrier`, and `CClosure` with `std`, turn it into a value first. - **Stable addresses.** A value C keeps a pointer to lives behind a pointer that does not move while C holds it: a `CBox`, a `CPayload`, a `CClosure` borrowed for the call. A by-value `Foo` or `CVal` moves, so C must not keep a pointer into one.

#!/bin/bash
# Build the safe crate's Rust static library for a variant's own C to link (crustify's
# porting-workflow skill, Builds): once a module has switched from C, the remaining C, its
# library, CLI and tests, reaches the module through the crate's exports, and its CMake
# build links this library (`LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY`).
#
#   rust-staticlib.sh <variant> <archive>
#
# Run from the variant's build dir, configured and not yet built, as the first step of its
# `build` command in crustify/artifacts/build.json; <archive> is the library written,
# relative to the build dir, as its configure's `-DLIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY` names it. The crate
# is the one of the checkout this script belongs to, built as a `staticlib` on the dev
# profile, the campaign's tests' own, in campaign mode against this build dir
# (`CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR`) with `CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB` set, so that it reads the build's headers
# and configuration and links none of its C, and with the `bindgen` feature, so that the
# committed bindings are checked against them. Its Rust is instrumented as
# crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh instruments <variant>'s, so that one runtime serves the C
# and the Rust of every C consumer. Cargo's target dir is the build's own, `crustify/cargo`;
# the archive is replaced atomically, so that a link never reads a partial one.
set -euo pipefail
usage='usage: rust-staticlib.sh <variant> <archive>'
variant=${1:?$usage}
archive=${2:?$usage}
[ $# -eq 2 ] || { echo "$usage" >&2; exit 2; }
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
[ -f CMakeCache.txt ] && [ -f build.ninja ] || {
  echo "rust-staticlib.sh: $PWD is not a configured CMake build with the Ninja generator" >&2
  exit 2
}
build=$(pwd -P)
case $archive in /*) ;; *) archive=$build/$archive ;; esac

export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR=$build CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB=1
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$build/crustify/cargo
crate=(-p libgit2-crustify --lib --locked --features bindgen)
bundled=
case $variant in
  plain)
    out=$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/debug
    "$here/crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh" "$variant" rustc "${crate[@]}" --crate-type staticlib ;;
  coverage|asan-ubsan|tsan)
    out=$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/$host/debug
    "$here/crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh" "$variant" rustc "${crate[@]}" --crate-type staticlib ;;
  bsan)
    # `cargo bsan` drives `build`, `run` and `test` only, and a `build` cannot change a
    # crate's type. It sets its rustc driver up and runs the cargo CARGO names, so a stand-in
    # for that cargo turns its `build` into `rustc --crate-type staticlib`, every other call,
    # its `metadata` among them, passing through. The /opt shim of `cargo bsan` sets CARGO
    # itself, so the real cargo-bsan, the ELF on PATH, is run directly, as the shim runs it.
    out=$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/bsan/$host/debug
    real_cargo=$(type -P cargo)
    real_bsan=
    for c in $(type -ap cargo-bsan); do
      [ "$(head -c4 "$c")" = $'\x7fELF' ] && { real_bsan=$c; break; }
    done
    [ -n "$real_bsan" ] || { echo "rust-staticlib.sh: no cargo-bsan executable on PATH" >&2; exit 1; }
    mkdir -p "$CARGO_TARGET_DIR"
    shim=$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/cargo-rustc-staticlib
    printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' \
      "[ \"\${1:-}\" = build ] || exec '$real_cargo' \"\$@\"" \
      'shift' \
      "exec '$real_cargo' rustc \"\$@\" --crate-type staticlib" >"$shim"
    chmod +x "$shim"
    side=$(realpath -m "$build/../../../..")
    export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
    export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
    (cd "$here" && RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=bsan CARGO=$shim "$real_bsan" bsan build "${crate[@]}")
    # The driver bundles BorrowSanitizer's C runtime into the library; the C's own links
    # link it (the variant's CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS), so that each process holds it once,
    # and a shared library none: its members are removed from the copy written.
    bundled=$(rustc +bsan --print sysroot)/lib/libclang_rt.bsan-x86_64.a
    [ -f "$bundled" ] || { echo "rust-staticlib.sh: no BorrowSanitizer runtime at $bundled" >&2; exit 1; } ;;
  *)
    echo "rust-staticlib.sh: unknown variant: $variant" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

lib=$out/liblibgit2_crustify.a
[ -f "$lib" ] || { echo "rust-staticlib.sh: cargo wrote no $lib" >&2; exit 1; }
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$archive")"
tmp=$archive.tmp.$$
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT
cp "$lib" "$tmp"
if [ -n "$bundled" ]; then
  mapfile -t members < <(ar t "$bundled" | sort -u)
  while ar t "$tmp" | grep -qxF -f <(printf '%s\n' "${members[@]}"); do
    ar d "$tmp" "${members[@]}"
  done
  ranlib "$tmp"
fi
mv -f "$tmp" "$archive"
trap - EXIT
echo "rust-staticlib.sh: $archive is the $variant Rust of $here"
#!/bin/bash
# Run the target's remaining C tests over a variant's build and compare them with the C test
# baseline (crustify's testing-gates skill, Regressions: a module's switch; setup, Baseline).
#
#   c-tests.sh <variant dir> <out dir> [jobs]
#
# <variant dir> is a built variant, crustify/builds/<variant>, whose C tests link the safe
# crate's Rust static library; its name is the variant whose record of
# crustify/artifacts/c-baseline.json the run is compared with. Nothing is written into it:
# every output goes under <out dir>.
#
# 1. build.json's `test` command, `ctest --output-on-failure -R '^(offline|util)$'`, over a
#    copy of the variant's CTestTestfile.cmake tree, so that ctest's own records stay out of
#    the variant, beside the suites of step 2: <out dir>/ctest.log, its exit status in
#    <out dir>/ctest.rc.
# 2. Every offline libgit2_tests suite and every util_tests suite alone, <jobs> side by side
#    (default 8), each under a 30-minute timeout, as the baseline ran them: TAP output in
#    <out dir>/suites/<binary>/<suite>.{tap,err,rc}. `online::*` suites need the network and
#    are left out, as the `offline` ctest target leaves them.
# 3. The tally, <out dir>/tally.json (cases passed, failed and skipped, and every suite that
#    failed a case or exited non-zero, with the sanitizer reports it printed), compared with
#    the baseline's record: the exit status is 0 when the case counts and the non-zero suites
#    (binary, suite, exit status) match it, and 1 otherwise, naming each difference. ctest's
#    status is reported beside it; under TSan the baseline's own races fail `offline`.
#
# The coverage variant's profiles go to /dev/null unless LLVM_PROFILE_FILE says otherwise.
set -uo pipefail
usage='usage: c-tests.sh <variant dir> <out dir> [jobs]'
d=$(cd -P "${1:?$usage}" && pwd) || exit 2
out=${2:?$usage}
jobs=${3:-8}
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)
variant=$(basename "$d")
[ -x "$d/libgit2_tests" ] && [ -x "$d/util_tests" ] || { echo "c-tests.sh: $d has no C tests built" >&2; exit 2; }
mkdir -p "$out"
out=$(cd -P "$out" && pwd)
export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-/dev/null}

# 1. ctest, over a copy of the test files: they name the executables by absolute path.
rm -rf "$out/ctest"
mkdir -p "$out/ctest"
(cd "$d" && find . -name CTestTestfile.cmake -not -path './crustify/*' -exec cp --parents {} "$out/ctest" \;)
# It runs beside the suites below, as one more job.
(
  ctest --test-dir "$out/ctest" --output-on-failure -R '^(offline|util)$' >"$out/ctest.log" 2>&1
  echo $? >"$out/ctest.rc"
) &
ctest_pid=$!

# 2. Every suite alone.
rm -rf "$out/suites"
for b in libgit2_tests util_tests; do
  mkdir -p "$out/suites/$b"
  "$d/$b" -l 2>/dev/null | sed -nE 's/^ *[0-9]+: (.*)$/\1/p' | grep -v '^online::' |
    D="$d" O="$out" B="$b" xargs -P "$jobs" -I{} bash -c \
      'cd "$O" && timeout 1800 "$D/$B" -t "-s$1" > "suites/$B/$1.tap" 2> "suites/$B/$1.err"; echo $? > "suites/$B/$1.rc"' _ {}
done

wait "$ctest_pid"

# 3. The tally, against the baseline.
python3 -I "$here/c-tests-tally.py" "$out" "$here/../artifacts/c-baseline.json" "$variant"
status=$?
echo "c-tests.sh: ctest exited $(cat "$out/ctest.rc") ($out/ctest.log)"
exit $status
Version 3: every variant links OpenSSL, PCRE2 and zlib from their side campaigns' installs of the same variant (../<source>-bindings/crustify/builds/<variant>/install), through OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR and CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH; libc stays the system's. Version 4: the coverage variant compiles with clang 23's source-based coverage (-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping). Version 5: libgit2 builds with -fvisibility=hidden, so libgit2.so exports only its GIT_EXTERN API; the last step of every variant's build, crustify/scripts/static-archive.sh, archives the objects libgit2.so links (its own TUs and the deps/ object libraries it bundles, as build.ninja's link edge lists them) into the variant's `static`, crustify/libgit2.a, which campaign mode links statically so that the Rust reaches libgit2's internal functions; the C tests and the CLI still link libgit2.so. Version 7: src/util/utf8.c, the first module switched from C, has left c/, and the C that remains, libgit2.so, the CLI and the C tests, links the safe crate's Rust static library, each variant's `rust`, which its configure names to the fork's CMake (-DLIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY) and the first step of its build makes (crustify/scripts/rust-staticlib.sh): the crate of the checkout CRUSTIFY_ROOT names, built as a staticlib on the dev profile in campaign mode against the configured variant, linking none of its C, and instrumented as cargo-variant.sh instruments the variant's Rust. libgit2.so keeps the Rust's symbols local (--exclude-libs), and campaign mode leaves the library out of the Rust's own links. 1://! `src/util/thread.c`: the threads, locks, atomics and thread-local storage libgit2 builds
2://! on, ported to Rust.
3://!
4://! # Atomics
5://!
6://! An [`Atomic32`] is a `git_atomic32` and an [`Atomic64`] a `git_atomic64` (`thread.h`): one
7://! integer, a `volatile int` and a `volatile int64_t`, that libgit2's threads share and change
8://! only through `thread.h`'s atomic operations, `git_atomic32_inc` and its siblings, each a
9://! sequentially consistent `__atomic` builtin in this build (`GIT_THREADS`, `GIT_BUILTIN_ATOMIC`).
10://! C embeds them by value: the reference count of every counted object (`git_refcount`, and
11://! `git_cached_obj`'s), a pack's and a pack file's counts, an index's readers, a transport's
12://! cancellation flag and the repository's attribute session key, and keeps a few as globals,
13://! the runtime's `init_count` and the object cache's `git_cache__current_storage`.
14://! [`AtomicSsize`] is `git_atomic_ssize`, an [`Atomic64`] where pointers are 64 bits wide.
15://!
16://! The value is the whole object, and its holders change it through shared access, so the
17://! handles lend it as the standard atomic it is, [`AtomicI32`](core::sync::atomic::AtomicI32) or
18://! [`AtomicI64`](core::sync::atomic::AtomicI64), through
19://! [`val`](Atomic32Ref::val): every Rust access is atomic, as every write C makes to one it
20://! shares is (C also zeroes them, with the storage that holds them, before sharing it). C also
21://! reads some of them plainly (`t->cancelled.val` in the smart transport,
22://! `git_cache__current_storage.val` in `git_libgit2_opts`), which races with an atomic write made
23://! on another thread as it races with C's own; nothing in Rust can make those reads atomic.
24://!
25://! A shared handle lends the atomic for writing, as `&AtomicI32` does, so a binding of a type
26://! that embeds one whose value C relies on, such as a reference count, lends its holders no
27://! handle to it, only what they may do with the value. A value Rust holds, as [`Atomic32::new`]
28://! builds it, lives in an [`UnsafeCell`](core::cell::UnsafeCell), so that it may be written
29://! through a shared borrow and a `static` of it is writable.
30://!
31://! `thread.h`'s operations over them are methods of the shared handles, each the one
32://! sequentially consistent operation C's is: [`Atomic32Ref::get`], [`set`](Atomic32Ref::set),
33://! [`inc`](Atomic32Ref::inc), [`dec`](Atomic32Ref::dec) and [`add`](Atomic32Ref::add), which
34://! return the value they leave, as C's do, and [`Atomic64Ref`]'s `get`, `set` and `add`, which
35://! are also `git_atomic_ssize`'s. Its operations over a pointer-sized slot,
36://! `git_atomic_compare_and_swap`, `git_atomic_swap` and `git_atomic_load`, are
37://! [`atomic_compare_and_swap`], [`atomic_swap`] and [`atomic_load`], over a standard
38://! pointer-sized atomic ([`AtomicWord`]), and its fence, `GIT_MEMORY_BARRIER`, is
39://! [`memory_barrier`]. C keeps them `static inline` in `thread.h`, which its own translation
40://! units expand, so the two operate on the same objects with the same instructions: C11's
41://! sequentially consistent atomics, which Rust's [`SeqCst`](core::sync::atomic::Ordering::SeqCst)
42://! are. The build is threaded (`GIT_THREADS`) with the `__atomic` builtins
43://! (`GIT_BUILTIN_ATOMIC`); its other branches, Windows' `Interlocked` calls, the older `__sync`
44://! builtins and the plain reads and writes of a build without threads, compute the same values
45://! for every input, with orderings no stronger than these.
46://!
47://! # Threads
48://!
49://! A [`Thread`] is a `git_thread` (`unix/pthread.h`): the `pthread_t` of a thread that
50://! `git_thread_create` starts into it and `git_thread_join` joins, C's only routines over it,
51://! both macros. C holds them by value, in the storage of what it hands each thread (the pack
52://! builder's `thread_params`, which it zeroes). Its one field is read by
53://! [`thread`](ThreadRef::thread) and written by [`set_thread`](ThreadMut::set_thread), which is
54://! `unsafe`: a join made through the object follows the id it stores. A zeroed value, as
55://! [`Thread::default`] gives, names no thread, as C's storage does before `git_thread_create`.
56://! A `pthread_t` joins once, so a [`Thread`] is neither `Clone` nor `Copy`.
57://!
58://! A thread Rust starts is native: [`spawn`] starts it, as `git_thread_create` does, and
59://! the [`JoinHandle`] it returns owns it, joined once by [`JoinHandle::join`], as
60://! `git_thread_join` joins, whose result is the closure's, as `pthread_join`'s `status` is the
61://! start routine's. A [`Thread`] stays the C form of a thread C starts into storage of its own,
62://! and a [`JoinHandle`] is never turned into one: the standard library cannot join a thread by
63://! its raw id, so only C could join it. The [locks](#locks) describe why these are native.
64://!
65://! # Locks
66://!
67://! [`Mutex`], [`Condvar`] and [`RwLock`] are `unix/pthread.h`'s `git_mutex`, `git_cond` and
68://! `git_rwlock`, which name `pthread_mutex_t`, `pthread_cond_t` and `pthread_rwlock_t`, their
69://! operations each the POSIX function of its name with default attributes. The header keeps
70://! them, and `git_thread_create` and `git_thread_join`, for the C that remains, which embeds its
71://! locks in its own structs and expands the macros where it locks them. The Rust forms are not
72://! linked to that C, and no lock or thread crosses between the two, so they are the standard
73://! library's: [`std::sync::Mutex`], [`std::sync::Condvar`], [`std::sync::RwLock`] and
74://! [`std::thread::Builder::spawn`], each behind a type of this module that carries its C names.
75://!
76://! Where C locks a lock and unlocks it later by name, Rust locks it into a guard, which its
77://! drop or its `unlock` releases: C's rule that a read lock is released with
78://! `git_rwlock_rdunlock` and a write lock with `git_rwlock_wrunlock` is the guard's type. A
79://! guard is not [`Send`], so a lock is released on the thread that took it, as POSIX requires
80://! of a default mutex and read-write lock. A lock guards the data it holds, a `T`, where C's
81://! guard state kept beside them: a lock of C's kind is a `Mutex<()>`.
82://!
83://! The standard locks differ from C's in three ways, none of which libgit2's C relies on:
84://!
85://! - They cannot fail to initialise, where `pthread_mutex_init` and its siblings may report
86://!   `EAGAIN` or `ENOMEM`, which libgit2 reports as an error: `new` is a `const fn`, and a lock may
87://!   be a `static`, as `GIT_RWLOCK_STATIC_INIT` initialises one in C.
88://! - A lock is poisoned when a thread panics while holding it, a state C has no form of: locking it
89://!   then fails with a [`PoisonError`], which hands back the guard, so that a caller that can vouch
90://!   for the data may go on with it. C's lock fails only with the errors POSIX lists, positive
91://!   numbers, which libgit2's callers test with `< 0` and so never see.
92://! - Taking a lock the calling thread already holds, a read lock included, deadlocks or panics,
93://!   where it deadlocks or is undefined in C: `unix/pthread.h` forbids recursive read locks for the
94://!   Windows implementation's sake.
95://!
96://! The macros are `unix/pthread.h`'s because this build defines `GIT_THREADS` and not
97://! `GIT_WIN32`. The branches it does not take compute the same: on Windows, `win32/thread.h`
98://! declares each as a function over a critical section, an event and a slim reader-writer
99://! lock, which exclude and wake as these do; without `GIT_THREADS`, `thread.h` makes each lock
100://! an `unsigned int` and each operation `git__noop_args`, returning 0, which excludes nothing
101://! because no second thread exists, and its `git_thread_create` and `git_thread_join` are only
102://! expanded under `#ifdef GIT_THREADS`.
103://!
104://! # Thread-local storage
105://!
106://! A [`TlsKey`] is a `git_tlsdata_key` (`thread.h`): a key made at run time, under which each
107://! thread keeps a value of its own, with a destructor that runs on each thread's value at that
108://! thread's exit. C keeps two, made at `git_libgit2_init`: `errors.c`'s, for each thread's
109://! error state, and `oid.c`'s, for `git_oid_tostr_s`'s per-thread string. C's `thread.c` builds
110://! them on POSIX keys (`pthread_key_create` and its siblings) where libgit2 is built with
111://! threads, as here; this module reimplements them over the standard library alone: a
112://! registry of the live keys, behind a lock, and one table per thread, in a `thread_local!`
113://! whose destructor runs the keys' destructors when the thread exits, a thread C started
114://! included. Each value holds its key's state beside it, so that reading or replacing a value
115://! and a thread's exit take no lock: the lock serves making and disposing of keys and a
116://! thread's first value of a key. A child forked from a threaded process may so run its
117://! thread-local destructors at `exit`, as libgit2's `git_process_start` does when its
118://! `execve` fails, without waiting on a lock that another thread of its parent held. The
119://! values never leave the thread that stored them, so a key is `Send` and `Sync` whatever its
120://! values are.
121://!
122://! A key's value is typed, [`TlsKey<T>`](TlsKey), where C's is a `void *`, and its destructor,
123://! a [`TlsdataInitDestroyFn`], is a plain Rust function of the value. The C that remains
124://! reaches the same keys through the module's exports, `git_tlsdata_init`, `git_tlsdata_set`,
125://! `git_tlsdata_get` and `git_tlsdata_dispose`, once the module has switched; until then they
126://! compile only under the `ffi-export-src-util-thread-c` feature. A key C makes holds C's
127://! pointers and C's destructor, and no safe Rust reaches it: a [`TlsKey`] is made only by
128://! [`TlsKey::new`]. They keep POSIX's behaviour where C's callers can see it: a value is
129://! absent until a thread stores one, storing one destroys nothing, the destructor runs at a
130://! thread's exit on the values it still holds of the keys still live, and disposing of a key
131://! runs no destructor, on any thread. They depart from it where nothing in libgit2 relies on
132://! it:
133://!

135://!   zeroed `static` a C caller has not initialised yet, names no key: reading it gives nothing and

49://! A [`Thread`] is a `git_thread` (`unix/pthread.h`): the `pthread_t` of a thread that
50://! `git_thread_create` starts into it and `git_thread_join` joins, C's only routines over it,
51://! both macros. C holds them by value, in the storage of what it hands each thread (the pack
52://! builder's `thread_params`, which it zeroes). Its one field is read by
53://! [`thread`](ThreadRef::thread) and written by [`set_thread`](ThreadMut::set_thread), which is
54://! `unsafe`: a join made through the object follows the id it stores. A zeroed value, as
55://! [`Thread::default`] gives, names no thread, as C's storage does before `git_thread_create`.
56://! A `pthread_t` joins once, so a [`Thread`] is neither `Clone` nor `Copy`.
57://!
58://! A thread Rust starts is native: [`spawn`] starts it, as `git_thread_create` does, and
59://! the [`JoinHandle`] it returns owns it, joined once by [`JoinHandle::join`], as
60://! `git_thread_join` joins, whose result is the closure's, as `pthread_join`'s `status` is the
61://! start routine's. A [`Thread`] stays the C form of a thread C starts into storage of its own,
62://! and a [`JoinHandle`] is never turned into one: the standard library cannot join a thread by
63://! its raw id, so only C could join it. The [locks](#locks) describe why these are native.
64://!
65://! # Locks
66://!
67://! [`Mutex`], [`Condvar`] and [`RwLock`] are `unix/pthread.h`'s `git_mutex`, `git_cond` and
68://! `git_rwlock`, which name `pthread_mutex_t`, `pthread_cond_t` and `pthread_rwlock_t`, their
69://! operations each the POSIX function of its name with default attributes. The header keeps
70://! them, and `git_thread_create` and `git_thread_join`, for the C that remains, which embeds its
71://! locks in its own structs and expands the macros where it locks them. The Rust forms are not
72://! linked to that C, and no lock or thread crosses between the two, so they are the standard
73://! library's: [`std::sync::Mutex`], [`std::sync::Condvar`], [`std::sync::RwLock`] and
74://! [`std::thread::Builder::spawn`], each behind a type of this module that carries its C names.
75://!
76://! Where C locks a lock and unlocks it later by name, Rust locks it into a guard, which its
77://! drop or its `unlock` releases: C's rule that a read lock is released with
78://! `git_rwlock_rdunlock` and a write lock with `git_rwlock_wrunlock` is the guard's type. A
79://! guard is not [`Send`], so a lock is released on the thread that took it, as POSIX requires
80://! of a default mutex and read-write lock. A lock guards the data it holds, a `T`, where C's
81://! guard state kept beside them: a lock of C's kind is a `Mutex<()>`.
82://!
83://! The standard locks differ from C's in three ways, none of which libgit2's C relies on:
84://!
85://! - They cannot fail to initialise, where `pthread_mutex_init` and its siblings may report
86://!   `EAGAIN` or `ENOMEM`, which libgit2 reports as an error: `new` is a `const fn`, and a lock may
87://!   be a `static`, as `GIT_RWLOCK_STATIC_INIT` initialises one in C.
88://! - A lock is poisoned when a thread panics while holding it, a state C has no form of: locking it
89://!   then fails with a [`PoisonError`], which hands back the guard, so that a caller that can vouch
90://!   for the data may go on with it. C's lock fails only with the errors POSIX lists, positive
91://!   numbers, which libgit2's callers test with `< 0` and so never see.
92://! - Taking a lock the calling thread already holds, a read lock included, deadlocks or panics,
93://!   where it deadlocks or is undefined in C: `unix/pthread.h` forbids recursive read locks for the
94://!   Windows implementation's sake.
95://!
96://! The macros are `unix/pthread.h`'s because this build defines `GIT_THREADS` and not
97://! `GIT_WIN32`. The branches it does not take compute the same: on Windows, `win32/thread.h`
98://! declares each as a function over a critical section, an event and a slim reader-writer
99://! lock, which exclude and wake as these do; without `GIT_THREADS`, `thread.h` makes each lock
100://! an `unsigned int` and each operation `git__noop_args`, returning 0, which excludes nothing
101://! because no second thread exists, and its `git_thread_create` and `git_thread_join` are only
102://! expanded under `#ifdef GIT_THREADS`.
103://!
104://! # Thread-local storage
105://!
106://! A [`TlsKey`] is a `git_tlsdata_key` (`thread.h`): a key made at run time, under which each
107://! thread keeps a value of its own, with a destructor that runs on each thread's value at that
108://! thread's exit. C keeps two, made at `git_libgit2_init`: `errors.c`'s, for each thread's
109://! error state, and `oid.c`'s, for `git_oid_tostr_s`'s per-thread string. C's `thread.c` builds
110://! them on POSIX keys (`pthread_key_create` and its siblings) where libgit2 is built with
111://! threads, as here; this module reimplements them over the standard library alone: a
112://! registry of the live keys, behind a lock, and one table per thread, in a `thread_local!`
113://! whose destructor runs the keys' destructors when the thread exits, a thread C started
114://! included. Each value holds its key's state beside it, so that reading or replacing a value

119://! values never leave the thread that stored them, so a key is `Send` and `Sync` whatever its
120://! values are.
121://!
122://! A key's value is typed, [`TlsKey<T>`](TlsKey), where C's is a `void *`, and its destructor,
123://! a [`TlsdataInitDestroyFn`], is a plain Rust function of the value. The C that remains

# Layout types whose state is written through shared access

Status: `open`.

## Signal

One representation written by hand (`evolution` §2), and a rule that forces a hand-written
layer `define_ctype!` could cover. `define_ctype!` lays a type out as its C struct alone,
`#[repr(transparent)] struct Foo(ffi::foo, PhantomData<…>)`. A value Rust holds hands out
its handles from `&self`, so they carry a pointer that may only be read through, as
`CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s documentation says. That is right for every C type whose writes go
through an exclusive handle. It is wrong for one whose state its holders change through
shared access, as an atomic counter's is: no write through a shared handle is sound over
a value Rust holds, and a `static` of such a type may be placed in read-only memory.

## Evidence

- `wave-226/batch-0/run-1`, `src/util/thread.c`, wraps `git_atomic32` and `git_atomic64`
  (`thread.h`): one `volatile int` or `int64_t` that libgit2's threads change only with
  `__atomic` builtins. Examples are every `git_refcount`, the runtime's `init_count`, and
  the object cache's `git_cache__current_storage`. The port batches that follow port
  `git_atomic32_inc` and its siblings over them, and the runtime's globals become Rust
  `static`s. Every write to these types goes through shared access.
- With `define_ctype!`, `Atomic32::new(0).as_ref().val().fetch_add(1, SeqCst)`, through
  `AtomicI32::from_ptr` on the projected field, is a write through a pointer derived from a
  shared borrow of a type with no `UnsafeCell`. That write is UB. `reproducer/`, beside this
  proposal, does it over ffibox `568bcb5`, and `cargo +nightly-2026-10-08 miri run` stops it:
  "Undefined Behavior: … only grants SharedReadOnly permission", the tag created by
  `define_ctype!`'s `as_ref`. Under Tree Borrows
  (`MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-tree-borrows`) the same run stops too: "write access through <509> …
  is forbidden … the conflicting tag <487> has state Frozen" (`wave-226/batch-4/run-1`, its
  review). The Reference counts the bytes a shared reference points at, outside an
  `UnsafeCell`, as immutable, so the write is UB in either model. So
  the run hand-wrote both layout types over `UnsafeCell<ffi::git_atomic32>`. It wrote one
  local `macro_rules!`, `atomic_type!` in `src/libgit2/src/util/thread.rs`, of about 140
  lines, which restates `define_ctype!`'s expansion: the layout type, both handles over
  `CBorrowedPtr`, `unsafe impl CCell`, the seams, and `as_ref` / `as_mut`. The only change
  is the `UnsafeCell`.
- `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s contract (ffibox `568bcb5`) lets nothing write the object while a
  shared handle lives, except through a `Mut` of the same borrow, or under a lock that
  every read through `Ref` takes. An atomic takes no lock. Each of its reads is atomic,
  and so is each concurrent write C makes. So the port's export of `git_atomic32_inc`
  adopts `a` as an `Atomic32Ref` while other C threads increment the same count. That keeps
  the atomics' own soundness argument, but not the trait's literal text. The record's row
  for `ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking` widened that text for a self-locking object; an
  object of atomics is the lock-free case of the same rule.
- G9's handle rule is "no Rust reference over foreign memory that anything may write
  while the reference lives". Read literally, it forbids the `&'a AtomicI32` the run's
  `val` accessor lends. The hazard G9 excludes is a reference that asserts what is false:
  immutability, or exclusive access. A shared reference to a standard atomic asserts
  neither. It asserts liveness, alignment, and that every concurrent access is atomic,
  which is the atomic's contract. The standard library offers `AtomicI32::from_ptr` for
  exactly this interoperation.

## Goal

Crustify's Safety goal (soundness), and ffibox's G1 (mirror standard Rust: a C atomic
field's safe form is the standard atomic) and G12 (obligations local: the contract an
atomics wrapper relies on is stated by the trait it implements, not argued against it).
The fitness measure: the hand-written `unsafe impl CCell` count in the campaign's crate,

Status: `open`.

## Signal

A tool that reports what the source contradicts (`evolution` §2). `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.borrow`
counts a raw pointer turned into a std reference through `<*const T>::as_ref`,

turns a `*mut T` into a `&'a Atomic…` the same way. The `ffimap` skill's Reviewing section

that starts from the scan misses every atomic lent over C memory.

### `libgit2/src/util/thread.c` wave 226 batch 3: thread-local storage and `git_threads_global_init`

A `port` batch of 7 items of `thread.c`, `thread.h` and `unix/pthread.h`, waves 226 and 227 folded
into one batch: `mac::git_tlsdata_key`, `fn::git_tlsdata_init`, `fn::git_tlsdata_set`,
`fn::git_tlsdata_get`, `fn::git_tlsdata_dispose`, `fnp::git_tlsdata_init.destroy_fn` and
`fn::git_threads_global_init`, in a section of their own in `thread.rs`. The keys are native, over
the standard library alone. A registry of the live keys sits behind a `Mutex`. Each thread keeps a
table in a `thread_local!`, whose drop runs the keys' destructors as the thread exits, a thread C
started included. `TlsKey<T>` stands in for the macro: a `Copy` id, `Send` and `Sync` whatever `T`
is, since no value leaves its thread. Its methods stand in for the four functions:
`new(Option<TlsdataInitDestroyFn<T>>)`, `set(Option<T>) -> Result<Option<T>, TlsError>`, which
hands back the value it replaces undestroyed, as C's does, `get() -> Option<T>` for `T: Clone`, and
`dispose()`. `TlsdataInitDestroyFn<T>` is the destructor, a plain `fn(T)`. `TlsError` reports
`KeysExhausted`, `Disposed` and `Unavailable`. `git_threads_global_init` is `global_init()`, which
does nothing on POSIX and returns nothing, since it cannot fail.

The keys keep POSIX's behaviour wherever C's callers can see it. A value is absent until stored and
after `NULL`. A store destroys nothing. The destructor runs at a thread's exit, on the values of live
keys alone. Disposing of a key runs no destructor on any thread. The module documentation records
where they depart from it. No key is 0, and no id is reused, so a zeroed `static` and a disposed
key's copies name no key. That ends the hazard of `crustify/LESSONS.md`'s first lesson for the
read: `threadstate_get` reads its key before `git_error_global_init` and, on POSIX, reads whatever
another component keeps under key 0. A destructor that stores again while its thread exits fails,
where POSIX would run the destructors again. Live keys are bounded only by 2³² − 1 ids, not by
`PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX`. The main thread's values are destroyed at `exit` too, as std's thread-locals
are on glibc. The keys C makes hold its pointers (`CWord`) and its destructor (`CDestructor`), both
in `ffi_import`, with the `thread_local!` itself, whose expansion is unsafe code. No safe Rust
reaches them. C's destructors free the value they are given, so they reach Rust through the export
alone, never as the callable type, as `binding-symbols` has it for a function whose argument is its
context. ffibox's `CFn` takes a context and is neither `Send` nor `Sync`, so the batch filed
`crustify/evolution/ffibox-cfn-without-context-on-any-thread`.

The module's export feature, `ffi-export-src-util-thread-c`, is declared off in `Cargo.toml`. Its
gateway exports the four `git_tlsdata_*` functions for `errors.c`, `oid.c` and
`threads/tlsdata.c`, each in ffibox's `barrier`, checked against its raw binding by a constant.
`allowlist.txt` gains the four functions (`bindings.rs` `+45`, with `pthread_key_t`, which `+LoC`
leaves out). `git_threads_global_init` stays `unix/pthread.h`'s `static inline` function, whose
address `git_libgit2_init` takes, with no export, as the task message has it. `porting-symbols`'
Static inline functions section would replace its definition by a prototype and export it at the
switch. As a scratch check, not a gate, the whole workspace built with the feature on, on `plain`,
links the exports in place of `thread.c.o`, whose only definitions they are, and passes. `lib`
has 914 tests, the gateway's two among them, then `equiv` 535, `ub_safe` 808, `ub_unsafe` 148,
`unit_pub` 266, and doctests 111 and 400. In that run, libgit2's own error state is on the Rust
keys. The pointer findings of `git_tlsdata_init`, `_set` and `_get` are in the ownership store.

Route confirmation (`dependencies.json`, libc): `pthread_key_create`, `pthread_key_delete`,
`pthread_getspecific` and `pthread_setspecific` are recommended `crustify-campaign`. glibc's wrapper
covers none of them, and neither does `nix`. The port uses none of them: the keys' state stays in
Rust and crosses to C only as the pointers C stores, so the route is `std` (`thread_local!` and
`Mutex`), as the Standard-library equivalents section gives it.

Tests: 16 `unit_pub` (`tests/unit_pub/src/util/thread/tlsdata.rs`), 5 `ub_safe`
(`tests/ub_safe/src/util/thread/tlsdata.rs`) and 4 `equiv` (`tests/equiv/src/util/thread/tlsdata.rs`).
There are also 5 `unit_priv` tests: the registry's ids, and C's keys with a C destructor, in
`ffi_import`. The gateway's own 2 compile under the feature. There are 4 doctests, 1 of them
compile-fail (`E0597`). `can_set_and_get` and `threads` carry over
`tests/libgit2/threads/tlsdata.c`'s two cases. The equivalence tests compare C's POSIX keys with
`TlsKey` step by step: values, failures, and the values each side's destructor runs on at its
threads' exits. They make no C call on a disposed key, which POSIX leaves undefined: a first version
did, and C's `git_tlsdata_set` succeeded, since glibc had given the index to another test's new key.
A key past `PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX` stands for C's key that names none.

The batch's tests pass plain, under ASan+UBSan and under TSan. Under Miri they all pass but the
`equiv` ones, each seen to stop at its first C call (`ignore = "calls C"`), and the doctests pass
too. BSan was not run: no test of this batch passes a pointer that Rust reborrows. The workspace
passes on `plain`, as do the module's and its 38 dependents' tests under ASan+UBSan, 1,202 of them,
selected by test path. The format check and the lints pass with the feature off and on. Everything

# Builds in this repository run the raw bindings in campaign mode, against the `plain`
# variant unless CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT names another, or is set empty to build as a
# dependent would (crustify's `bindgen` skill, Build modes).
[env]
CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT = "plain"
# pcre2-sys links the PCRE2 that pkg-config finds, else builds its vendored copy, which would
# shadow the side campaign's for libgit2's C too: point it at the variant's install
# (crustify/evolution/bundled-pcre2-shadows-the-side-campaign). cargo-variant.sh sets
# another variant's, which this does not override. The install is reached as the variant's
# build found it, from crustify/builds/plain, which a worktree or a gate snapshot links to the
# repository's own: the kernel resolves the `..` past that link, so that every checkout
# reaches the clone beside the repository holding the builds.
PKG_CONFIG_PATH = { value = "crustify/builds/plain/../../../../pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/plain/install/lib/pkgconfig", relative = true }

# Dependency cooldown: the resolver holds back crate versions published in the last three
# days, so that an update never takes a release before the ecosystem has seen it. The
# committed Cargo.lock is unaffected; it applies to resolution only.
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"
#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
SKILL.md
end-gates
test_end_gates.py

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## Legend

- `module` / `wave` / `batch` — the batch's place in `schedule.json`: its wave's module and
  the wave and batch indices
- `objective` — `wrap` or `port`; `pass` — `first` for a translation batch, `review` for a
  review batch; `Σ first` / `Σ review` total each pass apart
- `types` / `symbols` / `fields` — the batch's scheduled units (callbacks count as
  symbols) and its types' assigned field accessors; a review row counts what it reviewed
- `$` / `tokens` / `wall` — the agent's computed cost (API-equivalent under
  subscription), its tokens in millions as `crustify usage` reports them, and its elapsed
  time, C rebuild included; `$/<unit>` divides `$` by the row's units
- `+LoC` — the landing's Rust insertions/deletions; `loc` — its `.rs` insertions
- `cov (C/Rust)` — line coverage after the landing, all test workloads in one run: C over
  the link unit's TUs, Rust over non-test sources; a `Σ` cell is the pass's last landing
- `+UB safe tests` … `+unit tests` — the tests the landing added, with its C/Rust coverage
  change in pp
- `+lifecycle` … `+misc`, `total` — the reports a review batch filed, by kind
- safety audit columns — the Safety audit's metrics, as a landing changed them
- API stability columns — the landing's items by how `ffimap api` classifies their consumer-facing API against its base: `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed`, `new`, and `→Replaces` for the anchors a port moved; `unattributed` the crate's public items no anchor reaches, by module; `reasons` the changed and removed items with the reason the batch recorded
- `cost` / `review cost` / `total` — a module's translation, review and combined cost;
  `module wall` — first launch to final gate; `Σ recorded agents` leaves the assistant
  out, `Σ campaign` adds it, without per-unit cells
- `UB safe tests` … `Unit tests` — `#[test]` functions per suite, each with the coverage of
  running it alone; `Total tests` — all four, whose coverage is one joint run's union,
  never the sum
- `total`, `ported` and `wrapped` types and symbols — the scheduled public-API units, and
  those with a `Replaces:` or a `Wraps:` anchor at the tip; `share` is of the total

# run.sh <repo> <package> <cov dir>: build a coverage-instrumented scratch copy of the safe
# crate against the `coverage` variant, its test items under #[coverage(off)], and run each
# suite alone into <cov dir>/prof/<suite>: lib, each integration test binary, and doc. Each
# binary links the variant's C statically, so its profiles count the C and the Rust alike.
# report.py then reads the figures (testing spec, Coverage), with the variant's static archive
# as the C object.
set -euo pipefail
repo=$1 pkg=$2 out=$3
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' "$repo/Cargo.toml")
tree=$out/tree
rm -rf "$out"; mkdir -p "$tree/crustify" "$out/prof"
(cd "$repo" && tar -cf - --exclude=./target --exclude=./crustify --exclude=./c --exclude=./.git .) | (cd "$tree" && tar -xf -)
ln -s "$repo/c" "$tree/c"
ln -s "$repo/crustify/artifacts" "$tree/crustify/artifacts"
ln -s "$repo/crustify/builds" "$tree/crustify/builds"
python3 "$(dirname "$0")/mark.py" "$tree/src" "$tree/src/lib.rs"
cd "$tree"
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=coverage CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$out/target
export RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage" RUSTDOCFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage -Z unstable-options --persist-doctests $out/doctests"
cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" --target $host --no-run --message-format=json 2>"$out/build.err" \
  | python3 -c 'import sys,json
for l in sys.stdin:
  try: d=json.loads(l)
  except: continue
  if d.get("reason")=="compiler-artifact" and d.get("executable") and d["target"]["kind"]!=["custom-build"] and d.get("profile",{}).get("test"): print(d["target"]["name"],d["target"]["kind"][0],d["executable"])' > "$out/bins.txt"
cat "$out/bins.txt"
while read -r name kind exe; do
  suite=$([ "$kind" = lib ] && echo lib || echo "$name")
  mkdir -p "$out/prof/$suite"
  echo "== $suite"
  LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/$suite/%p-%m.profraw" "$exe" --skip compile_fail > "$out/$suite.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in $suite"
  tail -3 "$out/$suite.log"
  "$exe" --list 2>/dev/null | grep -c ': test$' > "$out/$suite.count" || true
done < "$out/bins.txt"
mkdir -p "$out/prof/doc"
echo "== doc"
LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/doc/%p-%m.profraw" cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" --target $host --doc > "$out/doc.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in doc"
tail -3 "$out/doc.log"

content.content:
The fitness measure: the hand-written `unsafe impl CCell` count in the campaign's crate,
which this run raised by two. No `ub` or `contracts` finding should appear on a layout
type written through shared access.

## Destination

ffibox: `define_ctype!` (`src/macros.rs`), `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s and `CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s
contracts (`src/traits.rs`), `docs/borrows.md`'s conventions, `docs/hand-written.md`'s
scope, and G9's handle row in `docs/goals.md`. Once that lands, `binding-types`' Field accessors
section gains the case's line: a field C changes through shared access, with atomic
operations alone, is lent by the shared handle as the standard atomic of its width, and its
layout type is declared `interior`.

## Change

1. `define_ctype!` takes an option, `interior`, for a C type whose state its holders write
   through shared access. It lays the type out as
   `#[repr(transparent)] struct Foo(UnsafeCell<ffi::foo>, PhantomData<…>)`. Its `as_ref`
   then hands out a pointer that may be written through, as `UnsafeCell::get`'s does, and a
   `static` of it is writable. All else is unchanged: `CCell`, the handles and the seams.
   The layout type stays `!Sync` until the binding asserts `Sync`.
2. `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s contract admits a third kind of concurrent write. Beside writes
   through a `Mut` of the same borrow, and writes under a lock every read through `Ref`
   takes, it admits writes made atomically to bytes that every access through `Ref` makes
   atomically, of the same size. `CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s note extends to such a type: one
   declared `interior` may be written through `as_ptr` atomically, even when Rust holds
   the value.
3. G9's handle row and `docs/borrows.md`'s "No reference covers C memory anything may
   write" exempt a shared reference to a standard atomic over a field that only atomic
   accesses reach. Such a reference asserts no immutability and no exclusive access.

## Validation

Not made: this proposal is the binder's, and ffibox is outside its evolution scope. The
run's `atomic_type!` is the expansion that `interior` would emit. Its tests are evidence
for that expansion:

- `tests/unit_pub/src/util/thread.rs`, `tests/ub_safe/src/util/thread.rs` and
  `tests/ub_unsafe/src/util/thread.rs`;
- a `static` written from four threads; and
- shared handles and a lent `&AtomicI32` incremented from four threads at once.

They are clean under Miri and TSan. A change would add these as ffibox tests, with a
`compile_fail` case that a non-`interior` type still hands out a read-only pointer.

## Row

| change | from | landed as | signal | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `define_ctype!` takes `interior`, a layout over `UnsafeCell` for state written through shared access; `ref_from_ptr` admits atomic writes to bytes every `Ref` access reaches atomically; G9 exempts a reference to a standard atomic | `libgit2-crustify`, `ffibox-atomic-layout-types` | — | `git_atomic32` / `git_atomic64` were laid out by hand over `UnsafeCell`, since `define_ctype!`'s values hand out read-only pointers, and the adoption the atomics' port makes broke `ref_from_ptr`'s text | a hand-written `CCell` over `UnsafeCell`, or a `ub` finding of a write through a shared handle of a value Rust holds | — |

## Review

None yet.

2. `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s contract admits a third kind of concurrent write. Beside writes
   through a `Mut` of the same borrow, and writes under a lock every read through `Ref`
   takes, it admits writes made atomically to bytes that every access through `Ref` makes
   atomically, of the same size. `CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s note extends to such a type: one
   declared `interior` may be written through `as_ptr` atomically, even when Rust holds
   the value.
3. G9's handle row and `docs/borrows.md`'s "No reference covers C memory anything may
   write" exempt a shared reference to a standard atomic over a field that only atomic
   accesses reach. Such a reference asserts no immutability and no exclusive access.

## Validation

Not made: this proposal is the binder's, and ffibox is outside its evolution scope. The
run's `atomic_type!` is the expansion that `interior` would emit. Its tests are evidence
for that expansion:

- `tests/unit_pub/src/util/thread.rs`, `tests/ub_safe/src/util/thread.rs` and
  `tests/ub_unsafe/src/util/thread.rs`;
- a `static` written from four threads; and
- shared handles and a lent `&AtomicI32` incremented from four threads at once.

They are clean under Miri and TSan. A change would add these as ffibox tests, with a
`compile_fail` case that a non-`interior` type still hands out a read-only pointer.

## Row

| change | from | landed as | signal | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `define_ctype!` takes `interior`, a layout over `UnsafeCell` for state written through shared access; `ref_from_ptr` admits atomic writes to bytes every `Ref` access reaches atomically; G9 exempts a reference to a standard atomic | `libgit2-crustify`, `ffibox-atomic-layout-types` | — | `git_atomic32` / `git_atomic64` were laid out by hand over `UnsafeCell`, since `define_ctype!`'s values hand out read-only pointers, and the adoption the atomics' port makes broke `ref_from_ptr`'s text | a hand-written `CCell` over `UnsafeCell`, or a `ub` finding of a write through a shared handle of a value Rust holds | — |

## Review

None yet.
